decks.title: Electrochemistry — Part 1: Galvanic cells and electrode potentials
goals: Describe a galvanic cell, write its cell notation and identify the anode and cathode
Use standard electrode potentials to calculate standard cell EMF and predict whether a reaction is feasible
Apply the Nernst equation to electrodes and cells at 298 K
Relate cell EMF to the Gibbs energy change and the equilibrium constant

slides.heading: Electrochemistry
slides.body_md: Part 1 — getting electricity out of a chemical reaction, and measuring how strongly it wants to happen.

visual.alt: Flow: a spontaneous redox reaction, with oxidation and reduction separated, sends electrons through a wire to do electrical work

slides.narration: Namaste! Your phone, a torch, a car and even a pacemaker run on chemistry. Electrochemistry studies how chemical reactions produce electricity, and how electricity can drive reactions that would not happen by themselves. In this part we build a cell from two metals, measure electrode potentials, and see how the voltage of a cell is linked to concentration, to Gibbs energy and to the equilibrium constant.

slides.heading: Two kinds of electrochemical cell
slides.body_md: In a **galvanic (voltaic) cell** a spontaneous redox reaction produces electricity. In an **electrolytic cell** electrical energy drives a non-spontaneous reaction. In both, **oxidation occurs at the anode** and **reduction at the cathode**.

visual.alt: Table comparing galvanic and electrolytic cells: energy change, reaction, sign and process at each electrode, and examples

slides.narration: There are two kinds of electrochemical cell. A galvanic cell lets a spontaneous reaction push electrons through a wire, so chemical energy becomes electrical energy. An electrolytic cell does the reverse: a battery forces a reaction that would not go on its own. One rule never changes. Oxidation always happens at the anode and reduction at the cathode. Only the signs of the electrodes swap between the two kinds of cell.

visual.caption: Zinc is the anode (oxidation, negative); copper is the cathode (reduction, positive).

slides.narration: Here is the classic galvanic cell, the Daniell cell. A zinc rod stands in zinc sulfate solution and a copper rod in blue copper sulfate solution. A wire joins the rods through a voltmeter, and a salt bridge joins the solutions. When both solutions are one molar, the voltmeter reads about one point one volts. Electrons leave the zinc, travel through the wire and arrive at the copper.

slides.heading: What happens in each half-cell
slides.body_md: Zinc is oxidised at the **anode**; copper ions are reduced at the **cathode**. The **salt bridge** (for example potassium chloride or ammonium nitrate in agar) completes the circuit and keeps both solutions electrically neutral.

rows: Positive charge builds up around zinc; negative around copper
Ions from the bridge move to cancel the charges
Solutions would mix if joined directly

visual.alt: Table contrasting a cell without a salt bridge, where charge builds up and current stops, with a cell with one, where ions keep the solutions neutral

slides.narration: At the zinc rod, zinc atoms lose two electrons and go into solution as zinc ions. That is oxidation, so zinc is the anode. At the copper rod, copper ions from the solution take two electrons and coat the rod with copper. That is reduction, so copper is the cathode. The salt bridge lets ions move between the beakers, so that charge does not pile up and stop the current.

slides.heading: Writing a cell in short form
slides.body_md: Convention: **anode on the left, cathode on the right**. A single vertical line separates phases; a double line is the salt bridge. Concentrations go in brackets.

visual.alt: Table of the conventions used when writing a cell: anode on the left, cathode on the right, single line for a phase boundary, double line for a salt bridge

slides.narration: Chemists write cells in a short form. The anode goes on the left and the cathode on the right. A single line marks a boundary between a solid and a solution, and a double line stands for the salt bridge. The cell voltage is then the potential of the right-hand electrode minus that of the left-hand electrode, that is, cathode minus anode.

slides.heading: Quick check: anode or cathode?
slides.body_md: In a cell written as Mg | Mg²⁺ || Ag⁺ | Ag, decide which electrode is oxidised.
slides.narration: Quick check. Use the cell notation rule: which side is the anode, and what process always happens at the anode?

slides.heading: Electrode potential and the reference electrode
slides.body_md: Each electrode has a tendency to gain or lose electrons, its **electrode potential**. Only differences can be measured, so every electrode is compared with the **standard hydrogen electrode (SHE)**, given a potential of exactly zero. **Standard** conditions: 1 M solutions, gases at 1 bar, 298 K.

rows: Copper ions are reduced more easily than hydrogen ions
Zinc is oxidised more easily than hydrogen

visual.alt: Table showing copper with a standard potential of plus 0.34 volts and zinc with minus 0.76 volts when measured against the standard hydrogen electrode

slides.narration: We cannot measure the potential of one electrode alone, just as we cannot measure the height of a hill without choosing sea level. So we choose a reference: the standard hydrogen electrode, given a potential of zero. Every other electrode is paired with it under standard conditions. Copper comes out at plus zero point three four volts and zinc at minus zero point seven six.

slides.narration: This is the reference electrode. A piece of platinum foil, coated with finely divided platinum black so that it has a large surface, dips into acid with a hydrogen ion concentration of one mole per litre. Pure hydrogen gas at one bar bubbles over it. The platinum only passes electrons in and out; the real electrode reaction is between hydrogen ions and hydrogen gas.

slides.heading: The electrochemical series
slides.body_md: Standard **reduction** potentials, listed in order. A **more positive** $E^\circ$ means the oxidised form is a **stronger oxidising agent**; a **more negative** $E^\circ$ means the metal is a **stronger reducing agent**.

visual.alt: Table of standard reduction potentials at 298 K from fluorine at plus 2.87 volts down to lithium at minus 3.05 volts

slides.narration: Here is a short electrochemical series, written as reductions. Fluorine at the top has the most positive value, so it grabs electrons most strongly: it is the strongest oxidising agent. Lithium at the bottom has the most negative value, so it gives electrons away most readily: it is the strongest reducing agent. A metal lower in the table can push the ions of a metal higher in the table out of solution.

slides.heading: Worked example: standard EMF of a cell
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find $E^\circ_\text{cell}$ for $\ce{Mg | Mg^2+ (1 M) || Ag+ (1 M) | Ag}$ and write the cell reaction.

**Step 1.** $E^\circ_\text{cell} = E^\circ_\text{cathode} - E^\circ_\text{anode} = 0.80 - (-2.37) = 3.17\ \text{V}$.

**Step 2.** Balance electrons: magnesium gives 2, each silver ion takes 1.

**Step 3.** $\ce{Mg(s) + 2Ag+(aq) -> Mg^2+(aq) + 2Ag(s)}$. The positive EMF shows the reaction is spontaneous.

visual.alt: Table of the silver and magnesium standard potentials and the resulting cell EMF of plus 3.17 volts

slides.narration: Take the cathode potential and subtract the anode potential. Silver is plus zero point eight, magnesium is minus two point three seven, so the difference is three point one seven volts. Notice that we never multiply a potential by the number of electrons; potentials are intensive. We only use the electrons to balance the overall equation: one magnesium atom reduces two silver ions.

slides.heading: Worked example: can you stir it with that?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Can silver nitrate solution be stirred with a nickel spatula? ($E^\circ$: $\ce{Ag+/Ag} = +0.80\ \text{V}$, $\ce{Ni^2+/Ni} = -0.25\ \text{V}$)

**Step 1.** Suppose nickel reacts: nickel would be the anode, silver ions the cathode.

**Step 2.** $E^\circ_\text{cell} = 0.80 - (-0.25) = 1.05\ \text{V}$, which is positive.

**Step 3.** So $\ce{Ni + 2Ag+ -> Ni^2+ + 2Ag}$ is spontaneous: the spatula would dissolve and silver would deposit. **No**, do not use it.

visual.alt: Flow for predicting a reaction: assume it happens, calculate the cell EMF, positive means it occurs, negative means it does not

slides.narration: To test whether a reaction happens, imagine it does, and work out the cell voltage. Nickel would be oxidised, so it is the anode; silver ions would be reduced at the cathode. The EMF is zero point eight minus minus zero point two five, which is one point zero five volts. A positive EMF means the reaction is spontaneous, so the nickel spatula would be eaten away.

slides.heading: Using the series to predict
slides.body_md: A metal with a lower (more negative) reduction potential displaces a metal ion with a higher one. Metals below hydrogen release hydrogen from dilute acids; metals above it do not.

rows: Does zinc displace copper from copper sulfate?
Does copper react with dilute hydrochloric acid?
Yes: chlorine is higher than bromine
Which is the stronger reducing agent, iron or magnesium?

visual.alt: Table of four predictions made from the electrochemical series about displacement, reaction with acid, oxidation of bromide and reducing strength

slides.narration: The series turns into a quick prediction tool. A metal that sits lower in the list, with a more negative potential, will displace the ions of a metal sitting higher. Metals with negative potentials push hydrogen out of dilute acids; copper and silver, with positive potentials, do not. In the same way, chlorine can pull electrons from bromide ions, because chlorine sits higher.

slides.heading: Quick check: strongest reducing agent
slides.body_md: Use the table of standard reduction potentials to pick the strongest reducing agent.
slides.narration: Quick check. A reducing agent gives away electrons. Look for the species that gives up electrons most readily: which end of the table is it at?

slides.heading: The Nernst equation for an electrode
slides.body_md: Electrode potentials change with concentration. For $\ce{M^{n+}(aq) + ne- -> M(s)}$, at $298\ \text{K}$:

visual.alt: Table of the symbols in the Nernst equation, with 2.303 RT over F equal to 0.059 volts at 298 kelvin

slides.narration: Standard potentials apply only at one molar. Real solutions are seldom exactly one molar, so Walther Nernst gave an equation to correct the potential. The correction term contains the gas constant, the temperature, the number of electrons and the Faraday constant, which is the charge on one mole of electrons. At twenty five degrees Celsius the whole group of constants becomes zero point zero five nine volts.

slides.heading: The Nernst equation for a cell
slides.body_md: For a cell reaction $\ce{aA + bB -> cC + dD}$ with $n$ electrons transferred, $Q$ is the reaction quotient (pure solids are left out).

rows: More copper ions (product side smaller Q)
EMF falls to zero (battery is flat)

visual.alt: Table of how changing the copper and zinc ion concentrations changes the EMF of the Daniell cell, falling to zero at equilibrium

slides.narration: For a whole cell, the Nernst equation uses the reaction quotient, which is products over reactants, leaving out pure solids. For the Daniell cell that is zinc ion concentration over copper ion concentration. If you increase copper ions, the quotient falls and the voltage rises. As the cell runs, zinc ions build up and copper ions are used, so the voltage falls, reaching zero at equilibrium.

slides.heading: Worked example: EMF at non-standard concentrations
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the EMF at $298\ \text{K}$ of $\ce{Zn | Zn^2+ (0.01 M) || Cu^2+ (1.0 M) | Cu}$, given $E^\circ_\text{cell} = 1.10\ \text{V}$.

**Step 1.** $n = 2$; $Q = \dfrac{[\ce{Zn^2+}]}{[\ce{Cu^2+}]} = \dfrac{0.01}{1.0} = 0.01$, so $\log Q = -2$.

**Step 2.** $E_\text{cell} = 1.10 - \dfrac{0.059}{2} \times (-2) = 1.10 + 0.059 = 1.159\ \text{V}$.

visual.alt: Table of n equal to 2, Q equal to 0.01, log Q equal to minus 2, and the cell EMF of 1.159 volts

slides.narration: Two electrons move in the Daniell reaction, so n is two. The quotient is zero point zero one over one, and its logarithm is minus two. Zero point zero five nine over two, times minus two, is minus zero point zero five nine, and subtracting a negative adds it. The EMF rises to about one point one six volts, because the product ions are scarce.

slides.heading: Worked example: pH from a hydrogen electrode
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A hydrogen electrode ($p_{\ce{H2}} = 1\ \text{bar}$) dipped in an acid solution has a potential of $-0.177\ \text{V}$ at $298\ \text{K}$. Find the pH.

**Step 1.** For $\ce{2H+ + 2e- -> H2}$: $E = 0 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{1}{[\ce{H+}]^2} = -0.059\,\text{pH}$.

**Step 2.** $\text{pH} = \dfrac{0.177}{0.059} = 3$.

visual.alt: Table of hydrogen electrode potential against pH: zero at pH 0, minus 0.177 volts at pH 3 and minus 0.413 volts at pH 7

slides.narration: A hydrogen electrode is really a pH sensor. Applying Nernst with two electrons and the square of the hydrogen ion concentration, the potential works out to minus zero point zero five nine times the pH. A reading of minus zero point one seven seven volts therefore means a pH of three. Each step of one pH unit shifts the potential by fifty nine millivolts.

slides.heading: Cell EMF, Gibbs energy and equilibrium
slides.body_md: The electrical work a cell can do equals the decrease in Gibbs energy. A **positive** $E_\text{cell}$ means a **negative** $\Delta G$: a spontaneous reaction. At equilibrium $E_\text{cell} = 0$, which links $E^\circ_\text{cell}$ to $K$.

visual.alt: Table linking the sign of the standard cell EMF to the sign of the standard Gibbs energy change and the size of the equilibrium constant

slides.narration: A cell can do electrical work equal to the fall in its Gibbs energy. So Gibbs energy change equals minus n times the Faraday constant times the cell EMF. A positive EMF means a negative Gibbs energy change and a spontaneous reaction. Because the EMF is zero at equilibrium, the standard EMF also tells us the equilibrium constant: a positive standard EMF of even one volt gives an enormous constant.

slides.heading: Worked example: ΔG° and K for the Daniell cell
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** For the Daniell cell, $E^\circ_\text{cell} = 1.10\ \text{V}$ and $n = 2$. Find $\Delta_\text{r}G^\circ$ and $K$ at $298\ \text{K}$. ($F = 96500\ \text{C mol}^{-1}$)

**Step 1.** $\Delta_\text{r}G^\circ = -2 \times 96500 \times 1.10 = -212300$, so $-212.3\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

**Step 2.** $\log K = \dfrac{2 \times 1.10}{0.059} \approx 37.29$.

**Step 3.** $K \approx 1.9 \times 10^{37}$: the reaction goes essentially to completion.

visual.alt: Table of the results: standard Gibbs energy change minus 212.3 kilojoules per mole and equilibrium constant about 1.9 times ten to the power 37

slides.narration: Multiply minus two by the Faraday constant by one point one zero, and you get about minus two hundred and twelve kilojoules per mole. That large negative value shows a very favourable reaction. For the equilibrium constant, two times one point one over zero point zero five nine is about thirty seven point three, so the constant is about ten to the power thirty seven. Zinc removes copper ions almost completely.

slides.heading: Quick check: signs
slides.body_md: A cell has a negative standard EMF. Decide what this means for the Gibbs energy change and the equilibrium constant.
slides.narration: Quick check. Use the relation between Gibbs energy and EMF, remembering the minus sign, and then think about what a positive Gibbs energy change means for the equilibrium constant.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Galvanic cell: spontaneous redox → electricity; anode (oxidation) negative, cathode (reduction) positive.
Salt bridge completes the circuit and keeps solutions neutral.
$E^\circ_\text{cell} = E^\circ_\text{cathode} - E^\circ_\text{anode}$; potentials are never multiplied by stoichiometric coefficients.
More positive E° → stronger oxidising agent; more negative → stronger reducing agent.
Nernst: $E_\text{cell} = E^\circ_\text{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{n}\log Q$ at 298 K.
$\Delta_\text{r}G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_\text{cell}$; $\log K = \dfrac{nE^\circ_\text{cell}}{0.059}$.

visual.alt: Summary table of the cell EMF, Nernst, Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant relations

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. A galvanic cell turns a spontaneous redox reaction into electricity, with oxidation at the anode and reduction at the cathode. The standard EMF is the cathode potential minus the anode potential. The Nernst equation corrects for concentration. And the EMF is tied to the Gibbs energy change and to the equilibrium constant, so one measurement of voltage tells us a lot about a reaction.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Never multiply E° by the number of electrons when balancing a cell reaction.
Write the anode on the left in cell notation; check that E°cell comes out positive for a working cell.
In the Nernst equation, Q is products over reactants; leave out pure solids and liquids.
Keep n the same in the Nernst equation and in ΔG° = −nFE°.
Give ΔG° in kJ mol⁻¹ by dividing joules by 1000, and keep the minus sign.

rows: E° is intensive: do not multiply
Q written as reactants over products

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: A few exam tips. Electrode potentials are never multiplied by the number of electrons, even when you double an equation. In cell notation, write the anode on the left. In the Nernst equation, the quotient is products over reactants, and pure solids are left out. Use the same n everywhere. And when you report a Gibbs energy change, convert joules to kilojoules and keep the minus sign.

decks.title: Electrochemistry — Part 2: Conductance, electrolysis, batteries and corrosion
goals: Define conductivity and molar conductivity and explain how they vary with concentration
Apply Kohlrausch’s law to find limiting molar conductivities and the degree of dissociation of weak electrolytes
Apply Faraday’s laws and predict the products of electrolysis
Describe primary and secondary batteries and the hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell, and explain corrosion and its prevention

slides.heading: Ions on the move
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how solutions conduct, how electricity makes new substances, how batteries store energy and why iron rusts.

visual.alt: Flow of the topics in Part 2: ions carry current, conductance, electrolysis, batteries and fuel cells, corrosion

slides.narration: In Part 2 the ions take centre stage. In a metal wire electrons carry the current, but in a solution ions do. We will measure how well a solution conducts, use conductance to study weak acids, apply Faraday’s laws to electrolysis, look inside batteries and fuel cells, and finally see why an iron gate rusts and how we can stop it.

slides.heading: Resistance, conductance and conductivity
slides.body_md: Resistance $R = \rho \dfrac{l}{A}$. Its reciprocal is **conductance** $G$ (unit siemens, S). The reciprocal of resistivity is **conductivity** $\kappa$ (kappa): the conductance of a solution between electrodes $1\ \text{cm}^2$ in area and $1\ \text{cm}$ apart.

visual.alt: Table of resistance, resistivity, conductance, conductivity and cell constant with their symbols and units

slides.narration: A solution resists current just as a wire does. Its resistance depends on the length between the electrodes and on their area. Conductance is simply one over resistance and is measured in siemens. Conductivity, written with the Greek letter kappa, is the conductance of a cube of solution one centimetre on each side. It depends on the electrolyte, its concentration and the temperature.

slides.heading: Measuring conductivity: the cell constant
slides.body_md: A **conductivity cell** has two platinised platinum electrodes a fixed distance apart. Its **cell constant** $G^* = \dfrac{l}{A}$ is found once using a potassium chloride solution of known $\kappa$. Alternating current is used, so that the solution is not electrolysed.

nodes.label: Fill cell with standard KCl solution
Measure R; find G* = κ × R

visual.alt: Flow for using a conductivity cell: calibrate with standard potassium chloride to find the cell constant, then measure the test solution

slides.narration: We cannot measure the length and area inside a real conductivity cell accurately, so we calibrate it. First we fill it with a potassium chloride solution whose conductivity is known, measure the resistance, and find the cell constant. After that, any solution’s conductivity is the cell constant divided by its resistance. Alternating current is used, so that no electrolysis happens at the electrodes during measurement.

slides.heading: Molar conductivity
slides.body_md: To compare electrolytes fairly, divide conductivity by concentration. **Molar conductivity** $\Lambda_\text{m}$ is the conductance of all the ions from one mole of electrolyte between electrodes 1 cm apart.

rows: Ions from one mole spread over more volume
Fewer charge carriers in each unit volume
Ions move more freely; weak electrolytes dissociate more

visual.alt: Table: on dilution conductivity decreases because there are fewer ions per unit volume, while molar conductivity increases

slides.narration: Conductivity alone is not a fair way to compare electrolytes, because a stronger solution simply has more ions. So we divide by concentration and get the molar conductivity. Watch the units: with conductivity per centimetre and concentration per litre, we multiply by one thousand. On dilution, conductivity falls, as there are fewer ions in each cubic centimetre, but molar conductivity rises.

slides.heading: Worked example: conductivity and molar conductivity
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A conductivity cell with cell constant $1.30\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ shows a resistance of $520\ \Omega$ when filled with $0.020\ \text{M}$ sodium chloride. Find $\kappa$ and $\Lambda_\text{m}$.

**Step 1.** $\kappa = \dfrac{G^*}{R} = \dfrac{1.30}{520} = 0.0025$, so $2.5 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{S cm}^{-1}$.

**Step 2.** $\Lambda_\text{m} = \dfrac{0.0025 \times 1000}{0.020} = 125$, so $125\ \text{S cm}^2\ \text{mol}^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Table of the data and results: cell constant 1.30, resistance 520 ohm, conductivity 0.0025 siemens per centimetre and molar conductivity 125

slides.narration: Divide the cell constant by the resistance: one point three over five hundred and twenty is two point five thousandths of a siemens per centimetre. For molar conductivity, multiply by one thousand and divide by the concentration, zero point zero two. The answer is one hundred and twenty five siemens square centimetre per mole. Always write the unit; it is part of the mark.

slides.heading: Strong and weak electrolytes on dilution
slides.body_md: **Strong** electrolytes: $\Lambda_\text{m}$ rises gently and linearly with dilution, $\Lambda_\text{m} = \Lambda^\circ_\text{m} - A\sqrt{c}$, so $\Lambda^\circ_\text{m}$ is found by extrapolation. **Weak** electrolytes: $\Lambda_\text{m}$ is low and rises steeply only at very low concentration, as dissociation increases; $\Lambda^\circ_\text{m}$ cannot be found by extrapolation.

points.label: Λ°m of ethanoic acid (not reachable by experiment)

visual.alt: Molar conductivity against the square root of concentration: potassium chloride falls along a gentle straight line from about 150; ethanoic acid is low at ordinary concentrations and rises steeply only on very great dilution towards 390.5
visual.caption: Strong electrolyte: extrapolate the straight line to zero concentration. Weak electrolyte: the curve cannot be extrapolated, so use Kohlrausch’s law.

slides.narration: Look at the two curves. For potassium chloride, a strong electrolyte, the molar conductivity falls in a nearly straight line as the square root of concentration rises, so we can extend the line back to zero concentration to find the limiting value. Ethanoic acid, a weak electrolyte, has a low molar conductivity that shoots up only on great dilution. Its limiting value cannot be read off the graph.

slides.heading: Kohlrausch’s law
slides.body_md: **Kohlrausch’s law of independent migration of ions:** the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the limiting molar conductivities of its cation and anion, each multiplied by the number of that ion in the formula.

visual.alt: Table of limiting molar conductivities of ions at 298 K, from hydrogen ion 349.6 and hydroxide 199.1 to ethanoate 40.9

slides.narration: Kohlrausch noticed that at infinite dilution each ion moves independently and makes its own fixed contribution. So the limiting molar conductivity of any electrolyte is just the sum of its ions’ contributions, each multiplied by how many of that ion the formula contains. Notice how large the values for hydrogen and hydroxide ions are: they move by a special hopping process through water.

slides.heading: Worked example: Λ°m of a weak base by Kohlrausch’s law
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** $\Lambda^\circ_\text{m}$ of $\ce{NH4Cl}$, $\ce{NaOH}$ and $\ce{NaCl}$ are $149.8$, $249.2$ and $126.4\ \text{S cm}^2\ \text{mol}^{-1}$. Find $\Lambda^\circ_\text{m}$ of $\ce{NH4OH}$.

**Step 1.** $\Lambda^\circ(\ce{NH4OH}) = \lambda^\circ(\ce{NH4+}) + \lambda^\circ(\ce{OH-}) = \Lambda^\circ(\ce{NH4Cl}) + \Lambda^\circ(\ce{NaOH}) - \Lambda^\circ(\ce{NaCl})$.

**Step 2.** $= 149.8 + 249.2 - 126.4 = 272.6$, so $272.6\ \text{S cm}^2\ \text{mol}^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Flow showing that adding the values for ammonium chloride and sodium hydroxide and subtracting sodium chloride leaves ammonium plus hydroxide

slides.narration: We cannot measure the limiting value for ammonium hydroxide directly because it is weak. But we can combine three strong electrolytes. Ammonium chloride plus sodium hydroxide gives ammonium, chloride, sodium and hydroxide. Subtracting sodium chloride removes the sodium and the chloride, leaving exactly ammonium and hydroxide. The answer is about two hundred and seventy three.

slides.heading: Worked example: degree of dissociation and Ka
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A $0.025\ \text{M}$ methanoic acid ($\ce{HCOOH}$) solution has $\Lambda_\text{m} = 33.0\ \text{S cm}^2\ \text{mol}^{-1}$. Using the ion values in the table, find $\alpha$ and $K_\text{a}$.

**Step 1.** $\Lambda^\circ_\text{m} = 349.6 + 54.6 = 404.2\ \text{S cm}^2\ \text{mol}^{-1}$.

**Step 2.** $\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_\text{m}}{\Lambda^\circ_\text{m}} = \dfrac{33.0}{404.2} \approx 0.0816$.

**Step 3.** $K_\text{a} = \dfrac{c\alpha^2}{1 - \alpha} \approx \dfrac{0.025 \times 0.0816^2}{0.918} \approx 1.81 \times 10^{-4}$.

visual.alt: Table of results for methanoic acid: limiting molar conductivity 404.2, degree of dissociation about 0.082 and acid constant about 1.8 times ten to the minus 4

slides.narration: For a weak acid, the ratio of the measured molar conductivity to the limiting value is the fraction of molecules that have split into ions. Kohlrausch gives the limit as hydrogen ion plus methanoate, four hundred and four point two. Dividing thirty three by that gives about eight percent dissociation. Putting this into the expression for the acid constant gives about one point eight times ten to the minus four.

slides.narration: Now we reverse the process and use electricity to cause a reaction. The battery pumps electrons into one electrode, the cathode, which becomes negative and attracts the cations; they gain electrons and are reduced. The other electrode, the anode, is positive; anions give up electrons there and are oxidised. Electroplating, refining of copper and the production of sodium and chlorine all use electrolysis.

slides.heading: Faraday’s laws of electrolysis
slides.body_md: **First law:** the mass of substance deposited or liberated is proportional to the charge passed, $m = ZIt$. **Second law:** for the same charge, masses of different substances are proportional to their molar masses divided by the number of electrons per ion. One mole of electrons carries **1 faraday**, $F \approx 96500\ \text{C mol}^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Table of the number of faradays needed per mole of silver, copper, aluminium and chlorine

math: Q = It, \qquad \text{moles of } e^- = \dfrac{Q}{F}, \qquad m = \dfrac{Q}{nF} \times M
slides.narration: Michael Faraday found two simple rules. The mass of product is proportional to the charge passed, which is current times time. And one mole of electrons, a charge of about ninety six thousand five hundred coulombs called one faraday, deposits one mole of silver, half a mole of copper or a third of a mole of aluminium, because those ions need one, two or three electrons each.

slides.heading: Worked example: silver plating
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A spoon is silver-plated using a current of $0.50\ \text{A}$ for $1930\ \text{s}$. What mass of silver is deposited? ($\ce{Ag+ + e- -> Ag}$, $M = 108\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$)

**Step 1.** $Q = It = 0.50 \times 1930 = 965$, so $965\ \text{C}$.

**Step 2.** Moles of electrons $= \dfrac{965}{96500} = 0.01$, so $0.01\ \text{mol}$ of silver.

**Step 3.** Mass $= 0.01 \times 108 = 1.08$, so $1.08\ \text{g}$ of silver.

visual.alt: Flow for a Faraday’s law calculation: charge from current and time, moles of electrons, moles of product, mass

slides.narration: First find the charge: half an ampere for one thousand nine hundred and thirty seconds is nine hundred and sixty five coulombs. Divide by the Faraday constant to get one hundredth of a mole of electrons. Each silver ion needs one electron, so one hundredth of a mole of silver is deposited. At one hundred and eight grams per mole, that is one point zero eight grams.

slides.heading: Predicting the products of electrolysis
slides.body_md: Products depend on the state of the electrolyte, the electrodes and the electrode potentials. In water, water itself may be reduced or oxidised instead of the ions. Some reactions are slower than their E° suggests and need an extra voltage, the **overpotential**; this is why chlorine, not oxygen, forms from concentrated brine.

visual.alt: Table of electrolysis products at the cathode and anode for molten and aqueous sodium chloride, dilute and concentrated sulfuric acid, and copper sulfate with copper or platinum electrodes

slides.narration: Which products form? With molten sodium chloride there is no water, so sodium forms at the cathode and chlorine at the anode. In aqueous solution, water competes. Water is reduced more easily than sodium ions, so hydrogen forms at the cathode. At the anode, oxygen should form in theory, but it needs a large overpotential, so chlorine forms from concentrated brine. With copper electrodes, the copper anode itself dissolves.

slides.heading: Batteries: primary and secondary
slides.body_md: A **primary** battery cannot be recharged: its reaction runs once. A **secondary** battery can be recharged by passing current in the opposite direction.

rows: Carbon rod with manganese dioxide; ammonium chloride and zinc chloride paste
Paste of mercury(II) oxide and carbon; potassium hydroxide and zinc oxide

visual.alt: Table of the dry cell, mercury cell, lead storage battery and nickel cadmium cell with their type, anode, cathode and electrolyte, and voltage

slides.narration: Batteries come in two families. A primary battery, like the dry cell in a television remote, runs its reaction once and is then thrown away. The mercury cell, used in hearing aids and watches, gives a very steady voltage because no ions in solution change concentration during its life. A secondary battery, like the lead storage battery in a car, can be recharged again and again.

slides.heading: The lead storage battery
slides.body_md: On **discharge**, both electrodes turn into lead sulfate and the sulfuric acid is used up, so its density falls. On **charging**, the reaction is reversed by an external supply.

visual.alt: Overall discharge reaction of the lead storage battery: lead plus lead dioxide plus two sulfuric acid gives two lead sulfate plus two water
visual.caption: Charging drives this reaction from right to left.

slides.narration: In a car battery, lead is the anode and lead dioxide is the cathode, both dipping in sulfuric acid. As the battery delivers current, both plates become coated with lead sulfate and the acid is used up, so the liquid becomes less dense. A mechanic can check the charge by measuring this density. When the engine runs, the alternator pushes current back and reverses the reaction.

Hydrogen is oxidised at one porous electrode and oxygen is reduced at the other, with hot alkali in between. The overall reaction is just hydrogen burning to water, but without a flame, so far more of the energy comes out as electricity. Spacecraft have used such cells and drunk the water they make.

slides.narration: Rusting is a tiny galvanic cell on the surface of iron. Under a drop of water, iron in one spot gives up electrons and dissolves. The electrons travel through the metal to another spot where oxygen from the air takes them, helped by hydrogen ions from dissolved carbon dioxide. The dissolved iron ions are oxidised further by air and form flaky, hydrated iron oxide: rust. Salt water speeds it up.

slides.heading: Preventing corrosion
slides.body_md: Corrosion is stopped by keeping oxygen and water away, or by making something else be oxidised instead of the iron.

rows: Paint, oil, grease or plastic keeps out air and water
Zinc coating; zinc is more reactive and corrodes first even when scratched
A block of a more active metal is joined to the iron and corrodes instead
Magnesium blocks on ship hulls and buried pipelines
Chemicals such as phosphates form a protective layer

visual.alt: Table of four methods to prevent corrosion: barrier coatings, galvanising, sacrificial anodes and anti-rust solutions, with how each works and examples

slides.narration: To stop rusting, we either shut out water and air, or make another metal corrode first. Paint and oil are simple barriers, but a scratch lets rust start. Galvanising coats iron with zinc, which has a more negative potential, so zinc is oxidised first even where the coat is broken. Ships and buried pipelines carry blocks of magnesium that slowly dissolve, sacrificing themselves to protect the steel.

slides.heading: Quick check: sacrificial protection
slides.body_md: Choose a metal that could protect an iron pipeline as a sacrificial anode.
slides.narration: Quick check. A sacrificial anode must be oxidised more easily than iron. Look for a metal with a more negative standard reduction potential.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: $\kappa = G^*/R$; $\Lambda_\text{m} = \kappa \times 1000 / c$ in $\text{S cm}^2\ \text{mol}^{-1}$.
On dilution κ decreases and Λm increases; strong electrolytes follow Λm = Λ°m − A√c.
Kohlrausch: $\Lambda^\circ_\text{m} = \nu_+\lambda^\circ_+ + \nu_-\lambda^\circ_-$; for a weak electrolyte $\alpha = \Lambda_\text{m}/\Lambda^\circ_\text{m}$.
Faraday: $m = \dfrac{ItM}{nF}$; $1\ F \approx 96500\ \text{C mol}^{-1}$.
Primary cells (dry, mercury) are not rechargeable; secondary cells (lead storage, nickel–cadmium) are.
Fuel cells convert fuel energy directly into electricity; corrosion is an electrochemical process prevented by barriers or sacrificial metals.

visual.alt: Summary table of the key relations in Part 2

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Conductivity comes from the cell constant and the resistance, and molar conductivity is conductivity per unit concentration. Kohlrausch’s law gives limiting values and the degree of dissociation of weak electrolytes. Faraday’s laws link charge to the mass of product. Batteries are primary or secondary, fuel cells run on a steady supply of fuel, and corrosion is a cell we try to stop.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: In $\Lambda_\text{m} = \kappa \times 1000/c$, κ must be in $\text{S cm}^{-1}$ and c in $\text{mol L}^{-1}$.
For Kohlrausch combinations, write the ions out and check that the unwanted ions cancel.
In Faraday problems, convert minutes to seconds and use the number of electrons per ion.
For brine electrolysis, mention overpotential to explain chlorine at the anode.
Galvanising protects even when scratched because zinc is more reactive (more negative E°) than iron.

Saying zinc coating is just a barrier
Zinc is oxidised in preference to iron

slides.narration: Some final tips. Watch the factor of one thousand in molar conductivity, and keep conductivity per centimetre and concentration per litre. In Kohlrausch problems, write out the ions so you can see them cancel. In Faraday problems, time must be in seconds. For brine, explain chlorine with overpotential. And remember that galvanising works because zinc is more reactive than iron, not only because it is a coat.

notes.title: Electrochemistry — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Galvanic cells and electrode potential
sections.body_md:
A **galvanic (voltaic) cell** converts the Gibbs energy of a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical energy. In the **Daniell cell**, zinc is oxidised at the **anode** ($\ce{Zn -> Zn^2+ + 2e-}$) and copper(II) ions are reduced at the **cathode** ($\ce{Cu^2+ + 2e- -> Cu}$); with 1 M solutions the EMF is 1.10 V. A **salt bridge** (KCl or $\ce{NH4NO3}$ in agar) completes the internal circuit and keeps the solutions electrically neutral.

**Cell notation:** anode | anode solution || cathode solution | cathode, e.g. $\ce{Zn(s) | Zn^2+(aq) || Cu^2+(aq) | Cu(s)}$. $E_\text{cell} = E_\text{right} - E_\text{left} = E_\text{cathode} - E_\text{anode}$.

**Electrode potential** is measured against the **standard hydrogen electrode** (Pt, platinum black, $\ce{H2}$ at 1 bar, $[\ce{H+}] = 1\ \text{M}$), assigned $E^\circ = 0$. Standard conditions: 1 M, 1 bar, 298 K. The **electrochemical series** lists standard reduction potentials: the more positive $E^\circ$, the stronger the oxidising agent (F₂ +2.87 V); the more negative, the stronger the reducing agent (Li −3.05 V). A metal with a lower $E^\circ$ displaces the ions of one with a higher $E^\circ$; metals with negative $E^\circ$ liberate hydrogen from dilute acids. $E^\circ$ values are **intensive**: never multiply them by stoichiometric coefficients.

sections.heading: 2. Nernst equation; Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant
sections.body_md:
For $\ce{M^{n+} + ne- -> M}$: $E = E^\circ - \dfrac{2.303RT}{nF}\log\dfrac{1}{[\ce{M^{n+}}]}$. At 298 K, $\dfrac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.059\ \text{V}$.

For a cell, $E_\text{cell} = E^\circ_\text{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{n}\log Q$, where $Q$ = products over reactants (pure solids omitted). For the Daniell cell $Q = [\ce{Zn^2+}]/[\ce{Cu^2+}]$. For a hydrogen electrode at 1 bar, $E = -0.059\,\text{pH}$.

**Gibbs energy:** $\Delta_\text{r}G = -nFE_\text{cell}$ and $\Delta_\text{r}G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_\text{cell}$ ($F = 96500\ \text{C mol}^{-1}$). Positive $E$ ⇒ negative $\Delta G$ ⇒ spontaneous.

**Equilibrium:** at equilibrium $E_\text{cell} = 0$ and $Q = K$, so $E^\circ_\text{cell} = \dfrac{0.059}{n}\log K$ and $\Delta_\text{r}G^\circ = -2.303RT\log K$. For the Daniell cell $\Delta_\text{r}G^\circ = -212.3\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $K \approx 10^{37}$.

sections.heading: 3. Conductance of electrolytic solutions
sections.body_md:
$R = \rho\dfrac{l}{A}$; conductance $G = 1/R$ (S); conductivity $\kappa = 1/\rho$ ($\text{S cm}^{-1}$ or $\text{S m}^{-1}$). In a conductivity cell, $\kappa = G^*/R$ where the **cell constant** $G^* = l/A$ is found with a standard KCl solution; alternating current is used.

**Molar conductivity** $\Lambda_\text{m} = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{c}$ ($\text{S cm}^2\ \text{mol}^{-1}$, with κ in S cm⁻¹ and c in mol L⁻¹). On dilution **κ decreases** (fewer ions per unit volume) but **Λm increases**.

- **Strong electrolytes:** $\Lambda_\text{m} = \Lambda^\circ_\text{m} - A\sqrt{c}$; $\Lambda^\circ_\text{m}$ by extrapolation to $c = 0$.
- **Weak electrolytes:** Λm rises steeply at low c because the degree of dissociation increases; $\Lambda^\circ_\text{m}$ cannot be extrapolated.

**Kohlrausch’s law:** $\Lambda^\circ_\text{m} = \nu_+\lambda^\circ_+ + \nu_-\lambda^\circ_-$. Uses: $\Lambda^\circ_\text{m}$ of weak electrolytes from strong ones (e.g. $\Lambda^\circ(\ce{NH4OH}) = \Lambda^\circ(\ce{NH4Cl}) + \Lambda^\circ(\ce{NaOH}) - \Lambda^\circ(\ce{NaCl})$); degree of dissociation $\alpha = \Lambda_\text{m}/\Lambda^\circ_\text{m}$; and $K_\text{a} = \dfrac{c\alpha^2}{1 - \alpha}$.

sections.heading: 5. Batteries and fuel cells
sections.body_md:
**Primary batteries** (not rechargeable): **dry (Leclanché) cell** — zinc container anode, carbon rod cathode with $\ce{MnO2}$, paste of $\ce{NH4Cl}$ and $\ce{ZnCl2}$; about 1.5 V. **Mercury cell** — Zn–Hg amalgam anode, HgO + carbon cathode, KOH/ZnO electrolyte; about 1.35 V, constant over its life because no ion concentration changes.

**Secondary batteries** (rechargeable): **lead storage battery** — Pb anode, $\ce{PbO2}$ cathode, about 38% $\ce{H2SO4}$. Discharge: $\ce{Pb + PbO2 + 2H2SO4 -> 2PbSO4 + 2H2O}$; the acid’s density falls. Charging reverses it. **Nickel–cadmium** cells last longer but cost more.

**Fuel cells** convert the energy of a fuel directly into electricity with continuous feed. **H₂–O₂ cell:** anode $\ce{2H2 + 4OH- -> 4H2O + 4e-}$, cathode $\ce{O2 + 2H2O + 4e- -> 4OH-}$, overall $\ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}$; about 70% efficient, pollution-free, used in spacecraft.

A cell that can be recharged by passing current in the reverse direction.

sections.heading: 6. Corrosion
sections.body_md:
**Corrosion** is the slow destruction of a metal by its surroundings; rusting of iron is an electrochemical process. At an **anodic** spot: $\ce{2Fe -> 2Fe^2+ + 4e-}$. Electrons flow through the metal to a **cathodic** spot: $\ce{O2 + 4H+ + 4e- -> 2H2O}$ ($\ce{H+}$ from $\ce{H2CO3}$ formed by dissolved $\ce{CO2}$). Overall: $\ce{2Fe + O2 + 4H+ -> 2Fe^2+ + 2H2O}$. $\ce{Fe^2+}$ is oxidised further to rust, $\ce{Fe2O3.xH2O}$. Salt water speeds corrosion by increasing conductivity.

**Prevention:** barrier coatings (paint, oil, grease, plastic); **galvanising** (zinc coat, which corrodes preferentially even when scratched); **sacrificial anodes** (magnesium or zinc blocks on ships and pipelines); anti-rust chemicals (e.g. phosphate coatings).

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Multiplying $E^\circ$ by the number of electrons when balancing a cell equation.
- Writing $E^\circ_\text{cell} = E^\circ_\text{anode} - E^\circ_\text{cathode}$ (it is cathode minus anode).
- Putting reactants over products in Q, or including pure solids.
- Forgetting the factor 1000 in $\Lambda_\text{m} = \kappa \times 1000/c$, or giving the wrong unit.
- Saying conductivity increases on dilution (it is molar conductivity that increases).
- Using minutes instead of seconds in $Q = It$.
- Saying oxygen forms at the anode in brine electrolysis without mentioning overpotential.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: correct option, sign, product or unit.
- Numericals (2–3 marks): formula (½–1) + substitution with units (1) + answer with unit (½–1).
- Cell questions: half-reactions (1) + overall reaction / notation (1) + EMF or prediction (1).
- 5-mark answers: often a definition or law, a labelled diagram (Daniell cell, SHE, fuel cell) and a numerical.

cards.front_md: Galvanic vs electrolytic cell?
cards.back_md: Galvanic: spontaneous reaction makes electricity. Electrolytic: electricity drives a non-spontaneous reaction.

cards.front_md: Which process happens at the anode?
cards.back_md: Oxidation — in every kind of cell.

cards.front_md: Two jobs of a salt bridge?
cards.back_md: Completes the circuit by letting ions move, and keeps both solutions electrically neutral.

cards.front_md: Write the Daniell cell in notation.
Formula for standard cell EMF?
cards.back_md: $E^\circ_\text{cell} = E^\circ_\text{cathode} - E^\circ_\text{anode}$ (right minus left).

cards.front_md: What is the SHE?
cards.back_md: Pt (platinum black) in 1 M $\ce{H+}$ with $\ce{H2}$ at 1 bar; $E^\circ = 0$ by definition.

cards.front_md: More positive E° means…?
cards.back_md: The oxidised form is a stronger oxidising agent (more easily reduced).

cards.front_md: Strongest reducing agent in the usual series?
cards.back_md: Lithium ($E^\circ = -3.05\ \text{V}$).

cards.front_md: Why does copper not give hydrogen with dilute HCl?
cards.back_md: Its $E^\circ$ (+0.34 V) is above that of hydrogen, so it cannot reduce $\ce{H+}$.

cards.front_md: Nernst equation for a cell at 298 K?
cards.back_md: $E_\text{cell} = E^\circ_\text{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{n}\log Q$.

cards.front_md: Potential of a hydrogen electrode in terms of pH?
Relation between ΔG° and E°cell?
cards.back_md: $\Delta_\text{r}G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_\text{cell}$.

cards.front_md: Relation between E°cell and K?
cards.back_md: $E^\circ_\text{cell} = \dfrac{0.059}{n}\log K$ at 298 K.

cards.front_md: What is E of a cell at equilibrium?
cards.back_md: Zero — the battery is flat.

cards.front_md: Define conductivity.
cards.back_md: Conductance of a solution between electrodes of $1\ \text{cm}^2$ area, $1\ \text{cm}$ apart; unit $\text{S cm}^{-1}$.

cards.front_md: What is the cell constant?
cards.back_md: $G^* = l/A$; found using a standard KCl solution; $\kappa = G^*/R$.

cards.front_md: Formula for molar conductivity?
cards.back_md: $\Lambda_\text{m} = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{c}$ in $\text{S cm}^2\ \text{mol}^{-1}$.

cards.front_md: Effect of dilution on κ and Λm?
cards.back_md: κ decreases (fewer ions per cm³); Λm increases.

cards.front_md: State Kohlrausch’s law.
cards.back_md: $\Lambda^\circ_\text{m} = \nu_+\lambda^\circ_+ + \nu_-\lambda^\circ_-$: each ion contributes independently at infinite dilution.

cards.front_md: Degree of dissociation from conductance?
cards.back_md: $\alpha = \Lambda_\text{m}/\Lambda^\circ_\text{m}$.

cards.front_md: Why use AC to measure conductivity?
cards.back_md: Direct current would electrolyse the solution and change its concentration at the electrodes.

cards.front_md: Faraday’s first law?
cards.back_md: Mass deposited ∝ charge passed: $m = ZIt$.

cards.front_md: Value of 1 faraday?
cards.back_md: About $96500\ \text{C mol}^{-1}$ — the charge on one mole of electrons.

cards.front_md: Products of electrolysis of concentrated brine (inert electrodes)?
cards.back_md: Hydrogen at the cathode, chlorine at the anode (oxygen has a high overpotential); NaOH stays in solution.

cards.front_md: Copper sulfate with copper electrodes — what happens?
cards.back_md: Copper deposits on the cathode and the copper anode dissolves (used in refining and plating).

cards.front_md: Primary vs secondary battery?
cards.back_md: Primary: cannot be recharged (dry cell, mercury cell). Secondary: rechargeable (lead storage, Ni–Cd).

cards.front_md: Why does a mercury cell give a constant voltage?
cards.back_md: The overall reaction involves no ions whose concentration changes during use.

cards.front_md: Overall discharge reaction of a lead storage battery?
cards.back_md: $\ce{Pb + PbO2 + 2H2SO4 -> 2PbSO4 + 2H2O}$.

cards.front_md: Advantages of an H₂–O₂ fuel cell?
cards.back_md: High efficiency (about 70%), continuous operation, only water as product.

cards.front_md: What is rust?
cards.back_md: Hydrated iron(III) oxide, $\ce{Fe2O3.xH2O}$.

cards.front_md: Why does galvanised iron not rust even when scratched?
cards.back_md: Zinc is more reactive (more negative E°) and is oxidised in preference to iron.

cards.front_md: Exam tip: E° and coefficients
cards.back_md: Never multiply E° by stoichiometric coefficients — it is an intensive property.

questions.stem_md: In the cell $\ce{Mg(s) | Mg^2+(aq) || Ag+(aq) | Ag(s)}$, which statement is correct?

options.text_md: Magnesium is reduced at the cathode.
Silver is oxidised at the anode.
Silver ions are oxidised at the cathode.
Magnesium is oxidised at the anode.

questions.solution_md: By convention the anode is written on the left, and oxidation always occurs at the anode, so magnesium is oxidised — option (d). Silver ions are reduced at the cathode on the right.

questions.stem_md: Standard reduction potentials: $\ce{Ag+/Ag} = +0.80\ \text{V}$, $\ce{Cu^2+/Cu} = +0.34\ \text{V}$, $\ce{Zn^2+/Zn} = -0.76\ \text{V}$, $\ce{Mg^2+/Mg} = -2.37\ \text{V}$. The strongest reducing agent among the metals is:
questions.solution_md: A reducing agent gives electrons; the metal with the most negative reduction potential loses electrons most readily. Magnesium (−2.37 V) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: $E^\circ(\ce{Ag+/Ag}) = +0.80\ \text{V}$ and $E^\circ(\ce{Zn^2+/Zn}) = -0.76\ \text{V}$. The standard EMF of $\ce{Zn | Zn^2+ || Ag+ | Ag}$ is:
questions.solution_md: $E^\circ_\text{cell} = E^\circ_\text{cathode} - E^\circ_\text{anode} = 0.80 - (-0.76) = 1.56$, in volts — option (a). (b) ignores the sign of zinc’s potential, (c) doubles silver’s potential (potentials are never multiplied), and (d) subtracts the wrong way round.

questions.stem_md: $E^\circ$ values: $\ce{Ni^2+/Ni} = -0.25$, $\ce{Zn^2+/Zn} = -0.76$, $\ce{Pb^2+/Pb} = -0.13$, $\ce{Cu^2+/Cu} = +0.34$, $\ce{Ag+/Ag} = +0.80\ \text{V}$. Which metal will displace nickel from nickel sulfate solution?
questions.solution_md: A metal displaces nickel if it is a stronger reducing agent, i.e. has a lower $E^\circ$ than $-0.25\ \text{V}$. Only zinc ($-0.76\ \text{V}$) does: $E^\circ_\text{cell} = -0.25 - (-0.76) = 0.51\ \text{V} > 0$ — option (a). Lead (b) is just above nickel, so its cell EMF would be negative.

questions.stem_md: If the salt bridge of a working Daniell cell is removed, the voltmeter reading:

options.text_md: stays the same, because electrons still flow through the wire
drops to zero, because the internal circuit is broken and charge builds up in the solutions
doubles, because the solutions can no longer mix
reverses, because copper becomes the anode

questions.solution_md: Without the salt bridge, ions cannot move between the half-cells; positive charge collects around the zinc and negative around the copper, and the current stops at once — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The standard potential of $\ce{Ag+ + e- -> Ag}$ is $+0.80\ \text{V}$; for $\ce{2Ag+ + 2e- -> 2Ag}$ it is still $+0.80\ \text{V}$.

**Reason (R):** Electrode potential is an intensive property and does not depend on the amount of substance.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. Doubling the equation doubles ΔG° but also doubles n, so E° = −ΔG°/(nF) is unchanged; R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Calculate the standard EMF, in volts, of the cell $\ce{Fe | Fe^2+ (1 M) || Ag+ (1 M) | Ag}$. ($E^\circ$: $\ce{Fe^2+/Fe} = -0.44\ \text{V}$, $\ce{Ag+/Ag} = +0.80\ \text{V}$)
questions.solution_md: $E^\circ_\text{cell} = E^\circ_\text{cathode} - E^\circ_\text{anode} = 0.80 - (-0.44) = 1.24$, so $1.24\ \text{V}$.

marking_scheme.step: Cathode minus anode with signs, 1.24 V

questions.stem_md: True or false? In an electrolytic cell, the anode is the negative electrode.
questions.solution_md: False. In an electrolytic cell the anode is joined to the positive terminal of the supply, so it is positive; oxidation still occurs there.

questions.stem_md: State two functions of a salt bridge in a galvanic cell. Why is potassium chloride in agar a suitable filling?

answer.model_answer_md: A salt bridge completes the internal circuit by letting ions move between the half-cells, and it keeps each solution electrically neutral so that current continues to flow. Potassium chloride is suitable because its ions move at similar speeds and do not react with the electrode solutions; agar keeps it as a gel.

questions.solution_md: Two functions, then a reason for the choice of electrolyte.

marking_scheme.step: Completes the circuit; maintains electrical neutrality
Ions of similar mobility that do not react (agar as gel)

questions.stem_md: A zinc electrode in 1 M zinc sulfate is connected to a standard hydrogen electrode at 298 K. The voltmeter reads 0.76 V, and electrons flow from the zinc to the hydrogen electrode. What is the standard electrode potential of zinc, and why is the hydrogen electrode used for such measurements?

answer.model_answer_md: Electrons leave the zinc, so zinc is the anode and has the lower potential. Since the hydrogen electrode is 0 V, E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = 0 − 0.76 = −0.76 V. Only differences in potential can be measured, so the hydrogen electrode serves as an agreed reference, assigned exactly zero.

questions.solution_md: Use the direction of electron flow to decide the sign; the SHE is the zero reference.

marking_scheme.step: E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V with reasoning from electron flow
SHE is the zero reference because only differences are measurable

questions.stem_md: Can iron(II) sulfate solution be stored safely in a copper vessel? Justify using $E^\circ(\ce{Fe^2+/Fe}) = -0.44\ \text{V}$ and $E^\circ(\ce{Cu^2+/Cu}) = +0.34\ \text{V}$.

answer.model_answer_md: For copper to react, $\ce{Cu + Fe^2+ -> Cu^2+ + Fe}$ would need copper as anode: $E^\circ_\text{cell} = -0.44 - 0.34 = -0.78\ \text{V}$. The EMF is negative, so the reaction is not spontaneous. Yes, the solution can be stored in copper.

questions.solution_md: Assume the reaction happens and find the sign of the cell EMF.

marking_scheme.step: E°cell = −0.78 V for the assumed reaction
Negative, so no reaction: safe to store

questions.stem_md: A galvanic cell is built from an aluminium electrode in $1\ \text{M}$ aluminium ions and a nickel electrode in $1\ \text{M}$ nickel ions. ($E^\circ$: $\ce{Al^3+/Al} = -1.66\ \text{V}$, $\ce{Ni^2+/Ni} = -0.25\ \text{V}$) (a) Which electrode is the anode? (b) Write the cell in notation and the balanced cell reaction. (c) Calculate $E^\circ_\text{cell}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Aluminium has the more negative potential, so it is oxidised: **aluminium is the anode**.

(b) $\ce{Al(s) | Al^3+(aq, 1 M) || Ni^2+(aq, 1 M) | Ni(s)}$. Electrons balanced (6): $\ce{2Al + 3Ni^2+ -> 2Al^3+ + 3Ni}$.

(c) $E^\circ_\text{cell} = -0.25 - (-1.66) = 1.41\ \text{V}$.

questions.solution_md: Lower E° is the anode; balance electrons (2 × 3 = 3 × 2); cathode minus anode.

questions.stem_md: A cell reaction has a negative standard EMF at 298 K. Which is correct for this reaction?

options.text_md: ΔG° is negative and K is greater than 1.
ΔG° is positive and K is greater than 1.
ΔG° is zero and K equals 1.
ΔG° is positive and K is less than 1.

questions.solution_md: $\Delta_\text{r}G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_\text{cell}$: a negative $E^\circ$ gives a positive $\Delta G^\circ$, and $\log K = \dfrac{nE^\circ}{0.059}$ is negative, so $K < 1$ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: For a Daniell cell, which change increases the EMF?

options.text_md: Increasing the concentration of zinc ions
Increasing the concentration of copper(II) ions

questions.solution_md: $E = 1.10 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\ce{Zn^2+}]}{[\ce{Cu^2+}]}$. Raising $[\ce{Cu^2+}]$ lowers $Q$ and raises $E$ — option (b). More zinc ions (a) or dilute copper sulfate (d) raise $Q$; the size of a solid electrode (c) does not appear in $Q$.

questions.stem_md: A one-electron cell reaction has $E^\circ_\text{cell} = 0.118\ \text{V}$ at $298\ \text{K}$. Its equilibrium constant is:
questions.solution_md: $\log K = \dfrac{nE^\circ}{0.059} = \dfrac{1 \times 0.118}{0.059} = 2$, so $K = 10^{2} = 100$ — option (a). (b) stops at $\log K$; (d) uses the wrong sign.

questions.stem_md: For a two-electron cell reaction, $E^\circ_\text{cell} = 0.50\ \text{V}$. $\Delta_\text{r}G^\circ$ is ($F = 96500\ \text{C mol}^{-1}$):
questions.solution_md: $\Delta_\text{r}G^\circ = -nFE^\circ = -2 \times 96500 \times 0.50 = -96500$ J, that is $-96.5\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ — option (a). (b) uses $n = 1$, (c) drops the minus sign, and (d) uses $n = 4$.

questions.stem_md: True or false? When a galvanic cell reaction reaches equilibrium, the EMF of the cell becomes zero.
questions.solution_md: True. At equilibrium $\Delta_\text{r}G = 0$, so $E_\text{cell} = -\Delta_\text{r}G/(nF) = 0$: the cell can do no more work.

questions.stem_md: Calculate the EMF at $298\ \text{K}$ of the cell $\ce{Ni(s) | Ni^2+ (0.01 M) || Ag+ (0.001 M) | Ag(s)}$. ($E^\circ_\text{cell} = 1.05\ \text{V}$)

marking_scheme.step: Balanced reaction with n = 2 and Q = 10⁴ (squares [Ag⁺])

questions.stem_md: Calculate $\Delta_\text{r}G^\circ$, in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, for $\ce{Fe(s) + 2Ag+(aq) -> Fe^2+(aq) + 2Ag(s)}$, given $E^\circ_\text{cell} = 1.24\ \text{V}$ and $F = 96500\ \text{C mol}^{-1}$.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Two electrons are transferred, so $n = 2$.

Step 2 — $\Delta_\text{r}G^\circ = -2 \times 96500 \times 1.24 = -239320$ J $\text{mol}^{-1}$.

Step 3 — In kilojoules: $-239320 \div 1000 = -239.3$, so about $-239.3\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

questions.stem_md: Calculate $\log K$ at $298\ \text{K}$ for $\ce{Cu(s) + 2Ag+(aq) -> Cu^2+(aq) + 2Ag(s)}$. ($E^\circ$: $\ce{Ag+/Ag} = +0.80\ \text{V}$, $\ce{Cu^2+/Cu} = +0.34\ \text{V}$)
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — $E^\circ_\text{cell} = 0.80 - 0.34 = 0.46$, in volts; $n = 2$.

Step 2 — $\log K = \dfrac{nE^\circ}{0.059} = \dfrac{2 \times 0.46}{0.059} \approx 15.59$.

questions.stem_md: A hydrogen electrode ($p_{\ce{H2}} = 1\ \text{bar}$) dips into a solution of pH 10 at $298\ \text{K}$. Find its electrode potential in volts.
Use the Nernst equation to explain why the voltage of a Daniell cell slowly falls as it is used, and what its voltage is when it is completely "flat".

answer.model_answer_md: As the cell works, zinc ions are produced and copper ions are used up, so Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] keeps increasing and the term (0.059/2) log Q grows, lowering E. When the reaction reaches equilibrium, Q equals K and the EMF becomes zero: the cell is flat.

questions.solution_md: Relate the changing concentrations to Q in the Nernst equation; at equilibrium E = 0.

marking_scheme.step: Q increases as Zn²⁺ forms and Cu²⁺ is used, so E falls

questions.stem_md: For the cell $\ce{Zn(s) | Zn^2+ (0.1 M) || Ag+ (0.01 M) | Ag(s)}$ at $298\ \text{K}$: (a) write the cell reaction, (b) write the Nernst equation for the cell, and (c) calculate its EMF. ($E^\circ_\text{cell} = 1.56\ \text{V}$)
questions.solution_md: Square the silver ion concentration in Q because two silver ions appear in the balanced equation.

questions.stem_md: When a solution of a strong electrolyte is diluted, what happens to its conductivity (κ) and its molar conductivity (Λm)?
questions.solution_md: Dilution lowers the number of ions per unit volume, so κ falls; but the ions from one mole move more freely, so Λm rises — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A student finds $\kappa = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{S cm}^{-1}$ for a $0.020\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ solution and reports $\Lambda_\text{m} = \dfrac{\kappa}{c} = 0.0125\ \text{S cm}^2\ \text{mol}^{-1}$. Which is the correct value and the reason for the error?

options.text_md: $1.25 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{S cm}^2\ \text{mol}^{-1}$; the student should have divided by 1000
$12.5\ \text{S cm}^2\ \text{mol}^{-1}$; c must be converted to $\text{mol cm}^{-3}$, which brings in a factor of 1000

questions.solution_md: $\Lambda_\text{m} = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{c} = \dfrac{2.5 \times 10^{-4} \times 1000}{0.020} = 12.5$, in $\text{S cm}^2\ \text{mol}^{-1}$ — option (d). With κ per cm and c per litre, the 1000 converts litres to cm³.

questions.stem_md: $\lambda^\circ(\ce{Ca^2+}) = 119.0$ and $\lambda^\circ(\ce{Cl-}) = 76.3\ \text{S cm}^2\ \text{mol}^{-1}$. $\Lambda^\circ_\text{m}$ of calcium chloride is:
questions.solution_md: $\Lambda^\circ(\ce{CaCl2}) = \lambda^\circ(\ce{Ca^2+}) + 2\lambda^\circ(\ce{Cl-}) = 119.0 + 2 \times 76.3 = 271.6$ — option (c). (a) forgets the 2 chloride ions, (b) doubles calcium instead, and (d) subtracts.

questions.stem_md: Using $\lambda^\circ$ values (S cm² mol⁻¹): $\ce{H+}$ 349.6, $\ce{Na+}$ 50.1, $\ce{K+}$ 73.5, $\ce{OH-}$ 199.1, $\ce{Cl-}$ 76.3, which electrolyte has the highest limiting molar conductivity?
questions.solution_md: By Kohlrausch’s law: HCl $= 349.6 + 76.3 = 425.9$; NaOH $= 50.1 + 199.1 = 249.2$; KCl $= 73.5 + 76.3 = 149.8$; NaCl $= 50.1 + 76.3 = 126.4$. Hydrochloric acid is highest — option (c), thanks to the very mobile hydrogen ion.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The conductivity of a potassium chloride solution decreases when it is diluted.

**Reason (R):** The molar conductivity of a potassium chloride solution increases when it is diluted.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. But A is explained by the fall in the number of ions per unit volume, not by the rise in molar conductivity; R is a separate fact — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** $\Lambda^\circ_\text{m}$ of ethanoic acid cannot be found by extrapolating its graph of $\Lambda_\text{m}$ against $\sqrt{c}$ to zero concentration.

**Reason (R):** Ethanoic acid becomes a strong electrolyte at high dilution.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the curve rises steeply near zero concentration and cannot be extended reliably. R is false: ethanoic acid stays a weak electrolyte; its degree of dissociation only increases on dilution — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? According to Kohlrausch’s law, at infinite dilution each ion makes a definite contribution to the molar conductivity, whatever the other ion in the electrolyte.
questions.solution_md: True. This is the law of independent migration of ions: Λ°m = ν₊λ°₊ + ν₋λ°₋.

questions.stem_md: For a conductivity cell, the ratio of the distance between the electrodes to their area, l/A, is called the ___.
questions.solution_md: l/A is the **cell constant**, G*.

questions.stem_md: Match each quantity with its usual unit.
questions.solution_md: G is in siemens; κ = G × l/A is in S cm⁻¹; Λm = κ/c is in S cm² mol⁻¹; G* = l/A is in cm⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: A conductivity cell of cell constant $0.92\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ has a resistance of $400\ \Omega$ when filled with a $0.020\ \text{M}$ solution of an electrolyte. Find the molar conductivity in $\text{S cm}^2\ \text{mol}^{-1}$.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — $\kappa = \dfrac{G^*}{R} = \dfrac{0.92}{400} = 0.0023$, in $\text{S cm}^{-1}$.

Step 2 — $\Lambda_\text{m} = \dfrac{0.0023 \times 1000}{0.020} = 115$, so $115\ \text{S cm}^2\ \text{mol}^{-1}$.

questions.stem_md: Using $\lambda^\circ(\ce{Na+}) = 50.1$ and $\lambda^\circ(\ce{SO4^2-}) = 160.0\ \text{S cm}^2\ \text{mol}^{-1}$, find $\Lambda^\circ_\text{m}$ of sodium sulfate in $\text{S cm}^2\ \text{mol}^{-1}$.
questions.solution_md: $\Lambda^\circ(\ce{Na2SO4}) = 2 \times 50.1 + 160.0 = 260.2$, so $260.2\ \text{S cm}^2\ \text{mol}^{-1}$.

questions.stem_md: State Kohlrausch’s law of independent migration of ions and give one use of it.

answer.model_answer_md: At infinite dilution, the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the limiting molar conductivities of its cation and anion, each multiplied by its number in the formula. It is used to find Λ°m of weak electrolytes such as ethanoic acid from values for strong electrolytes, and hence their degree of dissociation.

questions.solution_md: State the law; one use: Λ°m of weak electrolytes, α or Ka.

questions.stem_md: Explain why, on dilution, the conductivity of a solution decreases while its molar conductivity increases.

answer.model_answer_md: Conductivity is the conductance of a fixed unit volume of solution; on dilution there are fewer ions in that volume, so κ falls. Molar conductivity counts all the ions from one mole; on dilution these ions are farther apart and move more freely (and weak electrolytes dissociate more), so Λm rises.

questions.solution_md: Contrast ions per unit volume with ions from one mole.

marking_scheme.step: κ: fewer ions per unit volume
Λm: ions from one mole move more freely or dissociate more

questions.stem_md: The conductivity of $0.010\ \text{M}$ methanoic acid is $5.00 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{S cm}^{-1}$. Using $\lambda^\circ(\ce{H+}) = 349.6$ and $\lambda^\circ(\ce{HCOO-}) = 54.6\ \text{S cm}^2\ \text{mol}^{-1}$, calculate (a) $\Lambda_\text{m}$, (b) the degree of dissociation and (c) the dissociation constant.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\Lambda_\text{m} = \dfrac{5.00 \times 10^{-4} \times 1000}{0.010} = 50.0\ \text{S cm}^2\ \text{mol}^{-1}$.

(b) $\Lambda^\circ_\text{m} = 349.6 + 54.6 = 404.2$; $\alpha = \dfrac{50.0}{404.2} \approx 0.124$.

(c) $K_\text{a} = \dfrac{c\alpha^2}{1 - \alpha} \approx \dfrac{0.010 \times 0.124^2}{0.876} \approx 1.75 \times 10^{-4}$.

questions.solution_md: Λm from κ, Λ°m by Kohlrausch, α as their ratio, then Ka = cα²/(1 − α).

questions.stem_md: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed with inert electrodes. The product at the cathode is:
questions.solution_md: At the cathode, water ($E^\circ = -0.83\ \text{V}$) is reduced far more easily than sodium ions ($E^\circ = -2.71\ \text{V}$), so hydrogen forms and hydroxide ions stay in solution — option (a). Chlorine (c) forms at the anode; sodium (b) forms only from molten sodium chloride.

questions.stem_md: The charge needed to deposit one mole of aluminium from $\ce{Al^3+}$ ions is ($F = 96500\ \text{C mol}^{-1}$):
questions.solution_md: $\ce{Al^3+ + 3e- -> Al}$ needs 3 mol of electrons: $3 \times 96500 = 289500$ C — option (c). (a) uses one electron, (b) divides by 3, and (d) uses two electrons.

questions.stem_md: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed using platinum electrodes. The products at the cathode and the anode are:

options.text_md: hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
copper at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
copper at the cathode and sulfur dioxide at the anode
copper at the cathode, and the anode dissolves

questions.solution_md: Copper(II) ions are reduced more easily than water, so copper deposits. Sulfate ions are very hard to oxidise, so water is oxidised to oxygen at the inert platinum anode — option (b). A dissolving anode (d) happens only with a copper anode.

questions.stem_md: Two cells containing silver nitrate and copper(II) sulfate are connected in series. If $1.08\ \text{g}$ of silver is deposited, the mass of copper deposited is (Ag = 108, Cu = 63.5):
questions.solution_md: Moles of electrons $= \dfrac{1.08}{108} = 0.01$; copper needs 2 per atom, so $0.005$ mol Cu $= 0.005 \times 63.5 = 0.3175$ g — option (d). (a) forgets the factor 2.

questions.stem_md: The charge carried by one mole of electrons, about 96500 C, is called one ___.
questions.solution_md: It is one **faraday** (F).

questions.stem_md: A current of $2.0\ \text{A}$ is passed through copper(II) sulfate solution for $30\ \text{min}$. Find the mass of copper deposited, in grams. (Cu = 63.5, $F = 96500\ \text{C mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — $Q = It = 2.0 \times 30 \times 60 = 3600$, in coulombs.

Step 2 — Moles of electrons $= \dfrac{3600}{96500} \approx 0.0373$; moles of Cu $= \dfrac{0.0373}{2} \approx 0.01865$.

Step 3 — Mass $= 0.01865 \times 63.5 \approx 1.18$, so about $1.18\ \text{g}$.

questions.stem_md: How long, in seconds, must a current of $5.0\ \text{A}$ flow through molten aluminium oxide (dissolved in cryolite) to produce $2.7\ \text{g}$ of aluminium? (Al = 27, $F = 96500\ \text{C mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Moles of Al $= \dfrac{2.7}{27} = 0.1$; each needs 3 electrons, so $0.3$ mol of electrons.

Step 2 — $Q = 0.3 \times 96500 = 28950$, in coulombs.

Step 3 — $t = \dfrac{Q}{I} = \dfrac{28950}{5.0} = 5790$, so $5790\ \text{s}$ (about 96.5 min).

questions.stem_md: In a school demonstration, concentrated brine with a few drops of phenolphthalein is electrolysed with graphite electrodes. The liquid near the cathode turns pink and a pale green gas collects at the anode. Explain both observations.

answer.model_answer_md: At the cathode water is reduced instead of sodium ions, giving hydrogen gas and hydroxide ions; the hydroxide makes the solution alkaline, so phenolphthalein turns pink. At the anode the green gas is chlorine: oxygen evolution needs a large overpotential, so chloride ions are oxidised instead.

questions.solution_md: Cathode: water reduced, OH⁻ formed. Anode: chlorine because of the overpotential for oxygen.

marking_scheme.step: Cathode: water reduced to H₂ and OH⁻, so pink
Anode: chlorine, because oxygen has a high overpotential

questions.stem_md: Two electrolytic cells containing silver nitrate solution and copper(II) sulfate solution are connected in series. A steady current deposits $2.16\ \text{g}$ of silver. (a) How much charge passed? (b) What mass of copper was deposited? (c) If the current was $0.25\ \text{A}$, for how long did it flow? (Ag = 108, Cu = 63.5, $F = 96500\ \text{C mol}^{-1}$)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Moles of Ag $= \dfrac{2.16}{108} = 0.02$, so $0.02$ mol of electrons: $Q = 0.02 \times 96500 = 1930$ C.

(b) The same charge deposits $\dfrac{0.02}{2} = 0.01$ mol Cu $= 0.01 \times 63.5 = 0.635$ g.

(c) $t = \dfrac{1930}{0.25} = 7720$ s (about 2.1 h).

questions.solution_md: Cells in series pass the same charge; use moles of electrons, then n for each metal.

questions.stem_md: Why does a mercury cell keep an almost constant voltage of about 1.35 V throughout its life?

options.text_md: Its electrodes are made of mercury, which does not react.
Its overall reaction involves no ion in solution whose concentration changes.
It is recharged automatically while in use.
Its electrolyte is acidic, so the voltage cannot fall.

questions.solution_md: In the overall reaction zinc amalgam and mercury(II) oxide give zinc oxide and mercury: no dissolved ion changes concentration, so Q, and hence E, stays constant — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A car has not started for some days. The density of its battery acid has fallen from $1.28$ to $1.15\ \text{g mL}^{-1}$. What does this show?

options.text_md: The battery is overcharged: extra sulfuric acid has formed.
The battery has discharged: sulfuric acid has been used up to form lead sulfate and water.
Water has evaporated from the battery.
Lead dioxide has formed on both plates.

questions.solution_md: Discharge: $\ce{Pb + PbO2 + 2H2SO4 -> 2PbSO4 + 2H2O}$. Acid is consumed and water forms, so the density falls — option (b). Evaporation (c) would raise the density; charging (a) would also raise it.

questions.stem_md: A crewed spacecraft on a two-week mission needs a steady electricity supply and also drinking water, with as little extra mass as possible. Which power source suits it best?

options.text_md: Lead storage batteries, which are recharged by the crew each night
Dry cells, because they give a constant 1.5 V
A small diesel generator, which burns fuel to drive a dynamo
A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell, which produces electricity continuously and gives water as its only product

questions.solution_md: The fuel cell runs as long as hydrogen and oxygen are supplied, is about 70% efficient, and its product, water, can be drunk — option (d). Lead batteries (a) are heavy and need a power source to recharge; dry cells (b) run down; a generator (c) needs air and makes exhaust.

Choose the correct option.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

Lead dioxide cathode in sulfuric acid; rechargeable

questions.stem_md: Write the electrode reactions of the hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell with an alkaline electrolyte, and give one advantage of fuel cells over thermal power plants.

answer.model_answer_md: Anode: $\ce{2H2 + 4OH- -> 4H2O + 4e-}$. Cathode: $\ce{O2 + 2H2O + 4e- -> 4OH-}$. Advantage: much higher efficiency (about 70% against about 40%), because chemical energy becomes electricity directly; also no polluting products.

questions.solution_md: Two half-reactions and one advantage.

answer.model_answer_md: Anode: $\ce{Pb + SO4^2- -> PbSO4 + 2e-}$. Cathode: $\ce{PbO2 + SO4^2- + 4H+ + 2e- -> PbSO4 + 2H2O}$. The mechanic measures the density with a hydrometer; a low reading shows the battery is discharged and needs charging, which reverses the reactions.

questions.solution_md: Write both half-reactions; link acid consumption to the fall in density.
